item.content: When fixing cursor pagination over non-unique ordering, append a unique non-nullable tie-breaker (e.g. `pk`) centrally in the shared default-ordering helper rather than patching each connection, so every default-ordered connection benefits at once.

Changing cursor composition (adding an ordering component) invalidates previously issued cursors. Call this out explicitly in the change description and consider whether clients need a migration/grace path, since the blast radius spans every client using default-sorted cursors.

For pagination bug fixes, write a test that walks multiple pages (first/second/third) over rows that tie on all ordering fields, asserting endCursor advances and hasNextPage eventually becomes False; this directly reproduces the skip/repeat failure modes.

When porting an upstream PR into a fork, read the upstream diff first and mirror its file layout, naming, and enforcement point (e.g. middleware vs resolver) rather than inventing a parallel design; reviewers reject reimplementations that diverge from the referenced PR.

Don't add speculative abstractions, helper layers, or extra config surface beyond what the issue/upstream PR requires — reviewers flag such additions as 'Unnecessary'. Keep the diff minimal and scoped to the requested behavior.

In Saleor, per-site settings must be resolved via `Site.objects.get_current()` (or the `get_site_promise` dataloader in GraphQL), never by reading `settings.SITE_ID` directly, since one process may serve multiple sites and SITE_ID may be unset. The threaded site cache is process-global and not invalidated on Site/SiteSettings saves, so tests should read back with `refresh_from_db` or call `Site.objects.clear_cache()` instead of assuming a cold/warm cache.

Making a DB-seeding fixture `autouse=True` can mask or break tests that assert on migration-seeded rows, and interacts badly with `django_db(transaction=True)` teardown that truncates tables. Prefer an explicit `get_or_create` helper called at the point of need (e.g. inside user-creation helpers) over a global autouse fixture.

When a data migration seeds a required row (e.g. a default CustomerType) that transactional-test teardown can wipe, provide an idempotent `get_or_create` helper and call it from every non-API creation path (test user factories, random_data generators) rather than relying on the migration row existing.

In Saleor, `django_db(transaction=True)` tests flush all tables on teardown, deleting rows created by data migrations (including the default CustomerType). With `--reuse-db` the DB then stays broken for later runs, so any code path needing the default row must recreate it via `get_or_create(is_default=True, defaults={...})`.

When deleting rows that other code paths delete via a shared helper, mirror the existing pattern: reuse the same `select_for_update` locking helper (e.g. `attribute_value_qs_select_for_update()`) and wrap the lock+delete in `transaction.atomic()`, since reviewers explicitly ask why a new deletion path skips the locking used by sibling paths.

Deleting an `AttributeValue` row does not delete its uploaded file from object storage; file-type values need `delete_from_storage_task`. If the issue is scoped to one entity (e.g. user deletion) but the file-orphaning is systemic across product/page/attribute deletion, don't bolt a partial fix into the narrow path — note it as a known limitation and propose a general follow-up PR.

When a deletion must clean up related rows that the FK cascade would otherwise remove first, call the cleanup helper explicitly before `queryset.delete()`/`instance.delete()` inside the same atomic block, and document in the helper's docstring that it must run before the parent rows are deleted.

When a permission check maps an enum/type to a required permission via a dict lookup, treat unmapped keys as fail-closed: either raise PermissionDenied with all mapped permissions (so a future type can't silently pass) or emit a row-level error, rather than letting a bare KeyError surface as a 500. Apply the same guard in every file that performs the lookup.

Don't remove a mutation's static `permissions` tuple and replace it with a post-resolution check without also adding a coarse pre-check (e.g. `check_any_attribute_type_permission`) that requires at least one of the mapped permissions; otherwise a user with none of the relevant permissions can reach the resolver and the per-type check becomes the only gate.

In Saleor, attribute mutations must resolve permissions from the attribute's `type`: `MANAGE_PRODUCT_TYPES_AND_ATTRIBUTES` for `PRODUCT_TYPE`, `MANAGE_PAGE_TYPES_AND_ATTRIBUTES` for `PAGE_TYPE`. Bulk mutations over mixed types require both, so resolve the distinct set of types from the DB (via `values_list('type'/'attribute__type', flat=True).distinct()`) before checking, and update the mutation's `description` to document the type-dependent permission.

When comparing GraphQL global IDs (strings) against DB primary keys (ints), normalize one side explicitly (e.g. `str(pk)` for DB pks or `int(pk)` for input pks) and annotate the input parameter's real type (e.g. `attr_pks: list[str]`); reviewers flag mismatched typing and prefer a simple set difference (`set(input) - set(found)`) over list comprehensions for the missing-pk check.

A pre-validation existence check does not eliminate the FK IntegrityError race: another request can delete the row between the check and the `.add()`/insert. Don't claim the crash is fully fixed unless the check and the write are wrapped in the same `transaction.atomic()` (or the write tolerates the race); note the residual race explicitly.

When adding a NOT_FOUND existence check to one mutation, mirror the error shape (field name, code, `params` key, message) of the sibling mutation that already implements it (e.g. `productAttributeAssign`) so clients and tests see consistent errors across mutations.

A `select_for_update()` queryset that is only assigned (never iterated, sliced, or used as a subquery) executes no SQL, so no lock is taken and the following write runs unlocked. Force evaluation inside the `transaction.atomic()` block with `list(qs.values_list('pk', flat=True))` (fetching only pks) before the `bulk_update`/write.

When adding a test that a lock is actually taken, use the `assert_locks_rows_before_write` fixture (saleor/tests/fixtures.py): it captures the block's queries and asserts an ordered `FOR UPDATE` query is emitted before the `UPDATE`, catching silently-unevaluated lock querysets.

In Saleor, all `*_qs_select_for_update()` lockers should order by `pk` for a consistent, stable lock acquisition order across code paths; ordering by a mutable field like `sort_order` is not a reliable deadlock-avoidance sequence. If a reordering routine needs a different order, align the locker with the other lockers (pk) rather than diverging.

When deprecating GraphQL enum values or subscription types, apply the deprecation at every surface that exposes them: the enum members (WebhookEventTypeEnum, WebhookEventTypeAsyncEnum, WebhookSampleEventTypeEnum) via `deprecation_reason=...` on the graphene enum value, and the corresponding subscription `graphene.Field(...)` declarations in subscription_types.py. Reviewers reject partial deprecations that leave one surface (e.g. subscriptions) undeprecated.

When porting an upstream deprecation PR, reuse the existing deprecation message constant (e.g. DEPRECATED_EXPORT_MUTATIONS) rather than retyping the reason string, and regenerate schema.graphql so the `@deprecated(reason: ...)` directives appear on every affected enum member; add a CHANGELOG entry enumerating the deprecated event types and subscription types.

Deprecating a mutation does not automatically deprecate the webhook events/subscriptions it emits. If the issue says 'complete the deprecation', grep for the event type names (e.g. PRODUCT_EXPORT_COMPLETED) across enum definitions and subscription_types.py and deprecate each occurrence, otherwise the removal in a later release is not legally justified.

In Saleor's GraphQL schema, deprecation surfaces differ by location: input fields and enum values accept a `deprecation_reason`/`@deprecated` directive only when the description embeds the DEPRECATED_IN_3X_INPUT marker verbatim (schema_printer.print_input_value converts it); type descriptions have no directive, so prefix with a plain 'DEPRECATED:' text and do NOT embed DEPRECATED_IN_3X_INPUT there, since print_description truncates at that marker and would drop the reason.

When deprecating a whole feature area (e.g. preorder), enumerate every surface in one pass: mutations, output types and their fields, input types and their fields, filters (ProductFilterInput/ProductWhereInput/OrderFilterInput/etc.), and error-code enum members; then list them all in the CHANGELOG so the later removal is justified. Grep the feature name across graphql/ to find filters and error codes that are easy to miss.

For enum-member deprecation, pass a callable `deprecation_reason` to `graphene.Enum.from_enum` that returns the reason only for the targeted member(s) and None otherwise, rather than deprecating the whole enum; this keeps the rest of the enum undeprecated while marking the legacy code.

When deprecating a set of related flags/fields, grep the whole graphql/ tree for each field name and deprecate every surface in one pass: output type fields, input type fields (create/update/bulk mutations), filter fields (AttributeFilter/AttributeWhere), and sort/order enums. Reviewers ask why a sibling flag in the same category (e.g. filterableInDashboard alongside storefront flags) was left undeprecated.

When a deprecation reason is shared across multiple fields, define it once as a module-level constant (e.g. STOREFRONT_FLAG_DEPRECATION_REASON) and reuse it, rather than retyping the string per field; keep separate constants when the wording differs by audience (storefront vs dashboard).

In Saleor, deprecating a filter field requires moving it out of the filter's `Meta.fields` list and declaring it explicitly as a `django_filters.BooleanFilter`/`BooleanWhereFilter` with a `help_text` that embeds DEPRECATED_IN_3X_INPUT plus the reason, since Meta.fields entries cannot carry deprecation text.

When a security/authorization check is added to a payment or redemption flow, return a single generic error message for every rejection reason (not found, wrong customer, deleted assignee) so the response never leaks card existence or balance; log the specific reason server-side instead.

Don't name a helper parameter after one of several possible source types (e.g. `checkout_user_id` when the caller passes `Checkout | Order`); name it for the value it actually holds (`user_id`) or derive it inside the helper, since reviewers flag the misleading name.

When a behavior change affects a documented user-facing flow (e.g. gift cards as a payment method), update the corresponding docs page and CHANGELOG entry in the same PR; reviewers explicitly request docs updates for externally visible behavior changes.

When widening a DB column length limit, define a single module-level constant (e.g. `URL_MAX_LENGTH = 2048`) and reference it in both the model field and the migration's `AlterField`, so the two can't drift; add a test that builds a value of exactly that length and asserts it round-trips through the API and DB.

When an issue asks to widen one column, don't also widen sibling columns or add validation for them in the same PR — reviewers will call it out of scope. Note the sibling columns as a follow-up instead, keeping the diff to the requested field(s) and their migration.

In PostgreSQL (>= 9.2), increasing a varchar length limit is a catalog-only change: no table rewrite, only a brief ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock. Mention this in the migration docstring so reviewers don't worry about downtime on large tables.

When adding a setting that names an importable callable (e.g. `ADVISORY_LOCK_NAMESPACE_IMPORT`), resolve it at startup in the AppConfig.ready() validator (mirroring `validate_jwt_manager`/`setup_announcements`) so a typo fails fast at boot instead of lazily inside a request; keep the lazy `import_string` only as the runtime accessor.

When serializing structural writes with a Postgres advisory lock, take the lock before any `select_for_update` row locks in the same transaction, use only transaction-scoped `pg_advisory_xact_lock` (pgbouncer-safe, auto-released), and refresh in-memory instance state (e.g. `instance._mptt_refresh()`) after acquiring the lock since the write's math may be computed from stale pre-lock values.

When a code path has two branches (e.g. `partial_rebuild` vs `needs_full_rebuild`), don't write tests that only exercise the common branch — reviewers ask for the rarely-hit branch to be covered too, and it is usually cheap to add.

When upgrading a single dependency, pin it exactly (`==X.Y.Z`) in pyproject.toml and regenerate uv.lock with `uv lock`/`uv sync` rather than hand-editing lock entries; the lock diff will pull in transitive bumps (e.g. httptools) that must be committed together.

Don't widen the version range or upgrade sibling dependencies when the issue asks to upgrade one package to a specific version; keep the change to that package's specifier plus the regenerated lockfile.

In Saleor, dependency versions are managed with uv: `pyproject.toml` holds the specifier and `uv.lock` holds resolved versions/hashes. `exclude-newer` in the uv config caps which releases are eligible, so newer versions may exist on PyPI but be intentionally excluded — don't 'upgrade further' than the issue requests.

When removing a deprecated API surface, grep the feature name across graphql/ and the domain layer to separate what to delete (GraphQL types, inputs, filters, error codes, resolvers, cleaning/save paths) from what must stay (domain logic, celery tasks, DB columns); state explicitly in the CHANGELOG which behavior is retained so reviewers don't assume the whole feature is gone.

When a CHANGELOG or PR description claims a retained behavior (e.g. 'a preorder with an end date is still deactivated automatically'), verify the claim against the code: variants without an end date never deactivate, so qualify the statement (e.g. 'a preorder with an end date set') rather than overstating it — reviewers flag inaccurate behavioral claims.

In Saleor, removing a deprecated GraphQL API does not remove the underlying DB columns or domain logic; the issue may explicitly defer the column drop to a later release. Keep the model fields, celery deactivation task, fulfillment guard and quantityAvailable calculation intact, and only delete the GraphQL-facing types/inputs/filters/resolvers and the write paths that set the deprecated fields.

When catching a third-party library exception (e.g. Pillow's DecompressionBombError) to convert it into a user-facing error, log the original exception message with context (filename, sanitized URL) via `logger.warning(..., extra={...})` and re-raise a generic, actionable message to the user; reviewers reject replacing the library's diagnostic detail with unactionable info like just the filename.

When a setting must be applied to a third-party library at import/startup time (e.g. `Image.MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS`), do it in the AppConfig.ready() (saleor/core/apps.py), not in the settings module; document that tests cannot override it via the `settings` fixture and must monkeypatch the library attribute directly.

When a validation change rejects user uploads, add a mutation-level end-to-end test (e.g. `productMediaCreate`) asserting the GraphQL error code and message, not just a unit test of the validator — reviewers ask for the user-facing path to be covered.

When a cleanup/behavior change applies to several entity types (product, variant, customer, page), add an explicit test for every entity type the code path covers, not just the ones that were easiest to set up; reviewers ask for the missing entity (e.g. pageUpdate) even when the shared helper is already exercised elsewhere.

When a new cleanup path deletes rows that another mutation (e.g. attributeValueDelete) deletes with webhook side effects, explicitly note the asymmetry (which webhooks fire on each path) in the PR description or a code comment rather than leaving reviewers to wonder whether events were overlooked.

When testing that a mutation deletes a detached row, also assert that sibling/unassigned rows of the same attribute are untouched, and that re-submitting the same value (same file URL) keeps the existing row instead of delete-and-recreate; these assertions pin down the exact cleanup scope.

When a size/limit check reads a declared header (e.g. Content-Length) and parses it with int(), handle both malformed values and negative/zero values: a negative int slips past a `> max` comparison and past a try/except that only catches ValueError. Validate `declared_size < 0` explicitly (or clamp) and decide whether a malformed header should be a permanent (no-retry) or retryable error — a garbage header is usually a server/proxy defect, so raising a retryable IOError/HTTPError is often more correct than a permanent ValueError.

When a streaming size check accumulates chunks (`tell() + len(chunk) > max`), add a test where multiple chunks sum to exactly the limit and are accepted, not only the failing case; an off-by-one in the accumulation expression only shows up on the boundary-success path.

When adding a rejection path that logs structured context (e.g. object pk, source URL) for one error type, check the sibling rejection paths in the same function (status-code, content-type, size) — reviewers flag inconsistent logging where some rejections carry context and others log nothing; either unify them under one `except ValueError` with `error_type: type(error).__name__` or note the unification as a follow-up PR.

When a staged column removal uses `SeparateDatabaseAndState`, keep the DB columns NOT NULL and give them a `db_default` (e.g. `db_default=False`, `db_default=0`) in the `database_operations` `AlterField`s rather than making them `null=True`: old pods still read the columns through non-nullable GraphQL fields, and the new ORM omits them from INSERTs, so a DB-side default is what keeps both versions writing valid rows during a rolling deploy.

A `TODO: drop the columns in X.Y` comment in a migration docstring is not enough for staged removals — migration guidelines require the follow-up to be tracked by an explicit issue. Open the follow-up issue for the column drop and reference its number/URL in the migration docstring, otherwise reviewers reject the PR.

When a removal changes a model's default ordering (e.g. dropping `storefront_search_position` from `Attribute.Meta.ordering`), the CHANGELOG entry must tell affected merchants what to do, not just state the new order: name the mutations that used to set the field, note that the corresponding sort enum value is gone too, and suggest a replacement (sort in the storefront, or keep the value in metadata). Also update any pagination/ordering tests that relied on the old order.

When a mutation can lose a race with a concurrent delete of a parent row, catch the FK `IntegrityError` around the child insert and re-check parent existence (`Model.objects.filter(pk=...).exists()`) to distinguish a lost race (return NOT_FOUND) from a genuine constraint bug (re-raise); don't rely on a pre-validation existence check alone.

Don't wrap a single-statement block in `transaction.atomic()` — reviewers flag it as unnecessary. Only add atomic when multiple operations must commit/rollback together (e.g. lock + write, or cleanup + delete).

When a test must observe a real DB constraint (e.g. FK IntegrityError from a concurrent delete), use `@pytest.mark.django_db(transaction=True)` so the insert actually hits the database; the default wrapping transaction hides constraint violations and the test passes vacuously.

When a fix changes a denormalized/derived column (e.g. Order.charge_status/authorize_status computed from total_gross_amount), add a cheap parametrized unit test next to the changed function covering every transition direction (e.g. OVERCHARGED->FULL, FULL->PARTIAL, FULL->OVERCHARGED), not just the one direction from the bug report; reviewers explicitly ask for all directions to be covered.

When a bug leaves existing rows in a wrong denormalized state, don't fold the data repair into the code fix: reviewers want the fix PR kept small and portable, with repairing already-affected rows (selection criteria, granted refunds, data migration vs management command with a dry-run report) deferred to its own PR.

In Saleor, Order.charge_status and authorize_status are denormalized columns derived from total_gross_amount and are only recomputed when a payment event arrives; for orders in ORDER_EDITABLE_STATUS the stored total is deliberately stale (draft mutations only set should_refresh_prices). Any code path that persists recalculated totals (e.g. process_order_prices) must include both statuses in update_fields, otherwise a paid order is frozen in a wrong status forever.

When a sort/pagination fix changes the cursor composition (e.g. adding a field to the cursor tuple), add a parametrized paging test that walks multiple pages in both directions (first+after and last+before) and asserts the full concatenated order matches the expected order; also cover a non-numeric attribute sort where the new cursor slot is None, since that is the representative regression case.

When a fix changes cursor composition, explicitly document in the CHANGELOG that previously issued cursors are rejected with 'Received cursor is invalid' and clients must restart from the first page; reviewers ask for this blast-radius note even when the fix itself is small.

In Saleor, sorting products by a numeric attribute must order by the numeric value, not the string representation (otherwise '10' sorts before '9'). A numeric attribute holds exactly one value per product, so any aggregate (MIN/MAX) yields the same result; use MIN and state this rationale in a comment so readers don't wonder about multiple values.

Don't rename or repurpose an existing shared GraphQL input type (e.g. `TranslationInput` -> `CategoryTranslationInput`) to add a new feature: it is a breaking change for every client referencing the old type and cannot ship in an already-released minor version. Introduce a new dedicated input type (e.g. `ProductMediaTranslationInput`) and leave the existing one untouched; if a rename is truly needed, target the next major/minor release and note it in the PR description.

When adding a new translatable model, don't copy-paste the full `TranslationField` body or redeclare fields that a base type already defines (e.g. `language` on `BaseTranslationType`). Reuse `TranslationField(..., description_suffix=ADDED_IN_3XX)` and put `ADDED_IN_3XX` only in `Meta.description` of new classes; add the suffix at the single call site where a new field is attached to an existing type, to avoid inflating the schema.

A single migration that alters/creates columns on two different tables in one transaction is rejected: split it into separate migrations per table. Also, any new non-nullable column added to an existing table must carry a `db_default` so the zero-downtime (rolling deploy) migration path works while old pods still insert rows.

When a reviewer says a test 'feels upside down' or asks 'could we make it simpler?', rewrite the test to follow the natural user story (create entity A with tag X, then create entity B with tag Y, then assert A still has X and B has Y) instead of asserting on internal queryset state; and if a sibling test already covers the same scenario, delete the redundant one rather than keeping both.

Django's `related_manager.set(...)` replaces the entire relation, so using it to attach new rows to a shared parent (e.g. a tag reused across batches) silently detaches previously linked rows. Use `add(*instances)` when the intent is to append links; reserve `set()` for cases where the full replacement is explicitly desired.

When fixing a bug that only affects a bulk mutation, verify whether the single-item sibling mutations (create/update) share the buggy code path; if they already use the correct call, state that explicitly in the PR description so reviewers don't ask for redundant fixes, and scope the diff to the bulk path.

In Saleor, the supported-versions table lives in SECURITY.md; when dropping an EOL release, bump both rows (e.g. `>= 3.21` -> `>= 3.22` and `< 3.21` -> `< 3.22`) so the supported floor and the unsupported ceiling stay consistent.

When removing an EOL version from the supported list, check whether the next version is also approaching EOL (reviewers may ask you to mention it); if the issue only asks to drop one version, keep the diff to that version and note the upcoming EOL in the PR description rather than preemptively dropping it.

When replacing a workflow's `on.pull_request.paths` filter with an in-job change check (so the job always reports and can be a required status check), extract the detection into a reusable composite action under `.github/actions/<name>/action.yml` with a single `additional-file-patterns` input (newline-separated regexes) and a `changed` output; call it from each workflow passing only its own workflow file pattern, rather than duplicating the pattern list per workflow.

When adding `if:` conditions to a job's steps, put them at the top of each step (immediately after `name`/`id`), not at the bottom — reviewers flag bottom-placed `if:` as unusual and hard to read. Also update pre-existing `if: always()` steps to `if: ${{ !cancelled() && <new condition> }}` so they don't run when the change check short-circuits.

In GitHub Actions, a workflow skipped by `on.pull_request.paths` filtering never creates a check run, so it cannot be a required status check without deadlocking PRs it doesn't match. Moving the filter into a job step (which always runs and exits early) makes the check always report. The checkout is shallow, so the detection step must `git fetch --depth=1 origin $BASE_SHA` before `git diff --name-only $BASE_SHA HEAD`, and assign the diff to a variable first so a git failure fails the step instead of being read as 'no changes'.

When adding a new field to a pydantic manifest schema (ManifestSchema) that is consumed by a dict-based install path, don't rely on the schema's field_validator for normalization: `clean_manifest_data` validates but discards the model, so the normalized value never reaches the dict. Normalize explicitly at the consumption point (e.g. a `normalize_<field>()` helper called in `install_app` and `AppFetchManifest`) and add tests for normalization in both paths.

Don't add a pydantic `field_validator` whose return value is never used (the validated model is discarded by the caller): reviewers flag it as dead code and ask for it to be removed. If normalization is needed, do it explicitly where the value is consumed; if validation is needed, make the validated model the source of truth.

In Saleor, `django.utils.text.Truncator` is the established helper for the 2048-char limit (used by `AppProblem.set_message`); it keeps 2047 original chars and appends a single '…' (U+2026). Prefer it over hand-rolled slicing for new truncation logic, and name truncation tests `*_too_long_*` (not `over_long`) to match existing conventions.

When a migration creates a default row, guard it with `if not settings.POPULATE_DEFAULTS: return` at the top of the migration function, mirroring the other 'create default' migrations; then make every downstream consumer (e.g. the post-migrate assignment task) tolerate the row's absence by catching the domain exception (NoDefaultCustomerType) and returning early with a log line, rather than assuming the row exists.

When a PR description claims a failure mechanism (e.g. 'get_or_create hits a duplicate key and retries forever'), verify the claim against the actual code before submitting: `get_or_create` does not fail on an existing row, so reviewers will ask you to explain the real mechanism. State the concrete failure (e.g. the row is created on a logical replica where it should not be, breaking the replica's assumptions) or drop the unverified explanation.

In Saleor, `settings.POPULATE_DEFAULTS` gates whether data migrations seed default rows (e.g. the default CustomerType in account.0103). When it is False (logical replicas), the migration must not create the row, and code paths that assume a default exists (e.g. `get_default_customer_type()` raising `NoDefaultCustomerType`, the `assign_default_customer_type_to_users_task`) must handle its absence gracefully.
